topics.name: Boiling point
topics.kicker: The temperature where a liquid turns to gas · For water at sea level, 100 °C
topics.briefing: A liquid’s boiling point is the temperature where it turns into gas all the way through, sending bubbles of vapor rolling up from inside. For water at sea level that’s 100 °C (212 °F), but on top of Mount Everest the thin air lets water boil at only about 70 °C. Different substances have different boiling points, which is how oil refineries separate crude oil into gasoline, kerosene, and other fuels.
topics.answerHtml: Boiling point (accept boiling temperature or normal boiling point; prompt on boiling; do not accept “vapor pressure”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Trouton’s rule says that for many liquids, the enthalpy of vaporization divided by this temperature in kelvins is roughly the same number. Liquids with stronger intermolecular forces, like the hydrogen bonds in water, have higher values of this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas throughout, which is 100 degrees Celsius for water at sea level.

tossups.p: Antifreeze in a car’s radiator lowers the coolant’s freezing point and also raises this temperature, so the coolant can get hotter without turning into a gas. Distillation separates the liquids in a mixture, such as the parts of crude oil, by differences in this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature at which a liquid’s vapor pressure equals the pressure around it.

tossups.p: The rise in this temperature equals a constant called K-sub-b times the molality of the dissolved particles, and water’s value of that constant is about 0.512 degrees Celsius per molal. Dissolving salt or sugar raises this temperature, a colligative property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, 100 degrees Celsius for pure water at sea level.

tossups.p: IUPAC [“EYE-yoo-pak”] defines a “standard” version of this temperature at a pressure of 1 bar, which puts water’s at about 99.6 degrees Celsius. On the Kelvin scale, water’s ordinary value of this temperature is 373.15.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, 212 degrees Fahrenheit for water at sea level, at which a liquid turns into a gas.

tossups.p: When Anders Celsius created his temperature scale in 1742, he put 0 degrees at this temperature for water and 100 degrees at water’s freezing point. On the summit of Mount Everest, water reaches this temperature at only about 70 degrees Celsius.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, which is lower on mountaintops because the air pressure is lower.

tossups.p: The old Réaumur [“RAY-oh-myoor”] temperature scale put water’s value of this temperature at 80 degrees. On a heating curve, this temperature shows up as a flat stretch, because the added heat turns liquid into gas instead of making it hotter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature at which a liquid’s vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure.

tossups.p: In the Leidenfrost [“LYE-den-frost”] effect, drops of water skitter across a pan far hotter than this temperature, riding on a cushion of gas. Chemists add porous chips to flasks so that liquids heated past this temperature form bubbles smoothly instead of suddenly erupting, a problem called bumping.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, which is 100 degrees Celsius for water at sea level.

tossups.p: A hypsometer [“hip-SOM-uh-ter”] estimates how high up a mountain you are by measuring water’s value of this temperature, which drops as you climb. Evaporation happens at a liquid’s surface at any temperature, but at this temperature bubbles of gas form all through the liquid.
tossups.r: For water at sea level, it is 212 degrees Fahrenheit. For 10 points, name this temperature, which is raised inside a pressure cooker.

tossups.p: Deep inside a geyser, the pressure of the water above raises this temperature, so the water there gets far hotter than it could at the surface before it suddenly flashes into steam. Liquid nitrogen’s value of this temperature is about minus 196 degrees Celsius.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas throughout.

tossups.p: Branched molecules have lower values of this temperature than their straight-chain isomers, so neopentane’s is far below pentane’s. In the alkanes, this temperature climbs as the carbon chains get longer, so methane through butane are gases at room temperature but pentane is a liquid.
tossups.r: Distillation separates liquids by differences in this temperature. For 10 points, name this temperature, 100 degrees Celsius for water at sea level.

tossups.p: The Clausius–Clapeyron [“klah-pay-RAWN”] equation can predict how this temperature changes when the outside pressure changes. Helium has the lowest value of this temperature of any element, about 4 kelvins, and liquid nitrogen’s is about minus 196 degrees Celsius.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature at which a liquid’s vapor pressure equals the pressure of the surrounding air.

tossups.p: Carbon dioxide has no value of this temperature at ordinary air pressure, because dry ice turns straight into gas without melting. On a heating curve, this temperature appears as a flat stretch while liquid turns into gas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, which water reaches at 212 degrees Fahrenheit at sea level.

tossups.p: An azeotrope [“ay-ZEE-uh-trohp”] is a mixture whose gas has the same makeup as its liquid at this temperature, so ordinary distillation cannot separate it. Oil refineries split crude oil into gasoline, kerosene, and other fuels using differences in this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, which is 100 degrees Celsius for pure water at sea level.

tossups.p: A spoonful of salt in a pot of pasta water raises this temperature by only a tiny fraction of a degree. Adding a nonvolatile solute always raises this temperature, an effect called a colligative property because it depends only on the number of dissolved particles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature, which is lower on mountaintops and higher inside a pressure cooker.

tossups.p: Hydrogen sulfide molecules are heavier than water molecules, yet hydrogen sulfide is a gas at room temperature, because water’s hydrogen bonds give it a much higher value of this temperature. Among similar compounds, bigger molecules usually have higher values of this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas throughout, 100 degrees Celsius for water.

trap.title: Temperature, not pressure
trap.body: This temperature and vapor pressure are two halves of one idea: a liquid reaches this temperature when its vapor pressure climbs to match the outside pressure. So clues about Raoult’s law or pressure cookers tempt players to say “vapor pressure,” and others mix this temperature up with the melting point or freezing point. Saying just “boiling” only earns a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen for “this temperature”: 100 °C for water, lower on mountains, raised by dissolved salt, and used to separate liquids by distillation. “This quantity” or “this pressure” that rises as a liquid warms means vapor pressure; solid turning to liquid means the melting point.
trap.line: Real answer line: Boiling point (accept boiling temperature; prompt on boiling; do not accept “vapor pressure”)

topics.name: Marie Curie
topics.kicker: Pioneer of radioactivity · First person to win two Nobel Prizes
topics.briefing: Marie Curie grew up in Warsaw, Poland, where women were not allowed to attend university, so she moved to Paris and became one of the greatest scientists in history. With her husband, Pierre, she discovered two new elements, polonium and radium, and she coined the word “radioactivity.” She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win two, in physics in 1903 and in chemistry in 1911.
topics.answerHtml: Marie Curie (accept Maria Skłodowska, Marie Skłodowska-Curie, or Madame Curie; prompt on Curie; do not accept “Pierre Curie” or “Irène Joliot-Curie”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a young woman, this scientist attended a secret “Flying University,” because the official university in her city did not admit women. She later named one of the elements she discovered after her homeland, which was then divided among three empires.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Polish-born scientist who discovered radium and won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry.

tossups.p: This scientist measured the tiny electric currents that uranium’s rays produce in air, using an electrometer built by her husband and his brother Jacques, who had discovered the piezoelectric effect. She was following up on Henri Becquerel’s 1896 discovery that uranium gives off mysterious rays.
tossups.r: She went on to discover polonium and radium. For 10 points, name this scientist who coined the word “radioactivity.”

tossups.p: In 1898, this scientist found that thorium also gives off radiation, independently of Gerhard Schmidt in Germany. She noticed that the uranium ore pitchblende was far more radioactive than its uranium alone could explain.
tossups.r: That led her to discover polonium and radium. For 10 points, name this first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

tossups.p: This scientist’s 1903 doctoral thesis was titled _Research on Radioactive Substances_. She did much of the work behind it with her husband in a drafty, leaky shed, where they processed tons of ore.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scientist who won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with her husband and the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry on her own.

tossups.p: In 1921, U.S. President Warren Harding presented this scientist with one gram of radium, bought with money raised by American women. She founded the Radium Institute in Paris, and a sister institute later opened in her hometown.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scientist, the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.

tossups.p: In 1995, this scientist’s remains were moved to the Panthéon [“pahn-tay-OHN”] in Paris, making her the first woman buried there for her own achievements. After her husband died in a street accident in 1906, she became the first woman to be a professor at the University of Paris.
tossups.r: She won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry. For 10 points, name this discoverer of polonium and radium.

tossups.p: This scientist was nearly left out of the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics until her husband insisted that her work be honored too. The couple processed tons of ore in a drafty, leaky shed to collect tiny amounts of a new, faintly glowing element.
tossups.r: That element was radium. For 10 points, name this Polish-born scientist who coined the word “radioactivity.”

tossups.p: This scientist died in 1934 of aplastic anemia, a blood disease probably caused by years of handling radioactive materials. Her daughter Irène and Irène’s husband, Frédéric Joliot [“zhoh-LYOH”], shared the 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scientist who discovered radium and polonium with her own husband, Pierre.

tossups.p: In 1910, this scientist and André-Louis Debierne isolated radium as a pure metal. She named radium after the Latin word for “ray,” and its compounds glow faintly in the dark.
tossups.r: Element 96, curium, is named for her and her husband. For 10 points, name this scientist who won two Nobel Prizes.

tossups.p: This scientist realized that radiation must come from inside atoms, because a sample’s radiation depended only on how much uranium it held, not on its chemical form. She built on Henri Becquerel’s discovery of the rays given off by uranium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scientist, the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

tossups.p: In 1911, the French Academy of Sciences narrowly voted not to admit this scientist as a member. During World War I, she set up mobile X-ray units in cars to help army doctors treat wounded soldiers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this two-time Nobel Prize winner who discovered polonium and radium.

tossups.p: This scientist’s first research project in Paris studied the magnetic properties of different steels, and while looking for lab space for it, she met the French physicist she married in 1895.
tossups.r: With him, she later discovered polonium and radium. For 10 points, name this scientist who coined the word “radioactivity.”

tossups.p: This scientist and her husband chose not to patent their method for purifying radium, so that other scientists could use it freely. She founded the Radium Institute in Paris, which became a leading center for research on radiation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Polish-born scientist, the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.

tossups.p: In 1902, after years of processing pitchblende, this scientist finally isolated about a tenth of a gram of radium chloride. That ore was far more radioactive than its uranium could explain, which convinced her that it held new elements.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scientist who discovered polonium and radium and won Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry.

tossups.p: This scientist worked for years as a governess to help pay for her older sister Bronisława’s medical studies in Paris, before following her there to study physics. She named one of the elements she discovered after her homeland.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Polish-born scientist, the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

trap.title: Which Curie?
trap.body: Three Curies won Nobel Prizes: this scientist, her husband Pierre (who shared the 1903 Physics prize), and their daughter Irène Joliot-Curie (the 1935 Chemistry prize, with her husband Frédéric Joliot). Saying just “Curie” earns only a prompt, and naming the wrong family member loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Growing up in Warsaw, the Flying University, a second Nobel Prize in 1911, and naming polonium all mean this scientist. Pierre clues: piezoelectricity with his brother Jacques and the Curie temperature of magnets. Irène clues: making new radioactive elements and the 1935 prize. Always include her first name.
trap.line: Real answer line: Marie Curie (accept Maria Skłodowska; prompt on Curie; do not accept “Pierre Curie” or “Irène Joliot-Curie”)

topics.name: Solubility
topics.kicker: How much of a substance can dissolve · Why salt vanishes but sand doesn’t
topics.dates: Henry’s law for dissolved gases stated in 1803
topics.briefing: Stir salt into a glass of water and it vanishes, but keep adding more and eventually grains pile up at the bottom: you have reached salt’s solubility, the most of it that can dissolve in that much water. Chemists’ rule of thumb is “like dissolves like,” which is why salt dissolves in water but oil doesn’t. Most solids dissolve better in hot water, yet warm soda goes flat faster, because gases dissolve better in cold liquids.
topics.answerHtml: Solubility (accept word forms like soluble; prompt on dissolving or miscibility; do not accept “solubility product” or “Henry’s law”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the fountain experiment, water sprays into a flask of ammonia gas, because ammonia’s very high value of this property in water lets the gas dissolve and leave a partial vacuum. On graphs of this property against temperature, sodium chloride’s curve is nearly flat, while potassium nitrate’s rises steeply.
tossups.r: This property is often given in grams of solute per 100 grams of water. For 10 points, name this property, the maximum amount of a substance that can dissolve in a solvent.

tossups.p: Adding table salt to a saturated solution of silver chloride lowers this property of silver chloride, an example of the common-ion effect. For a salt that barely dissolves, chemists can calculate this property from a constant called K-sub-s-p, a product of the dissolved ions’ concentrations.
tossups.r: A saturated solution holds as much solute as this property allows. For 10 points, name this property, which tells how much of a solute can dissolve in a solvent.

tossups.p: Doctors can safely have patients swallow barium sulfate before X-rays of the digestive system, because this property is extremely low for that compound, even though dissolved barium ions are poisonous. Calcium hydroxide, the compound dissolved in limewater, has a lower value of this property in hot water than in cold water.
tossups.r: Stirring or crushing a solid makes it dissolve faster, but neither one changes this property. For 10 points, name this property, the greatest amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature.

tossups.p: Nutritionists group vitamins A, D, E, and K together because of this property in fats, which lets the body store them in the liver and fatty tissue. Vitamin C and the B vitamins are instead grouped by their high values of this property in water.
tossups.r: Substances with high values of this property in water are called hydrophilic, or “water-loving.” For 10 points, name this property, a measure of how well a substance dissolves.

tossups.p: In the “golden rain” demonstration, yellow lead(II) iodide is dissolved in hot water, and glittering golden crystals appear as the water cools, because this property of that compound is much lower in cold water. That compound first forms as a solid when solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide are mixed.
tossups.r: For most solids, this property rises in hotter water. For 10 points, name this property, the most solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent.

tossups.p: Henry’s law says that this property for a gas is proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid. For that reason, soft drinks are bottled under a high pressure of carbon dioxide, which comes fizzing out when the cap is opened.
tossups.r: Unlike most solids, gases have a lower value of this property in warm water, so warm soda goes flat faster. For 10 points, name this property, a measure of how much of a substance can dissolve.

tossups.p: Reusable hand warmers contain a sodium acetate solution holding more solute than this property normally allows, so clicking a metal disc inside makes the extra solute crystallize suddenly and give off heat. Rock candy grows from a sugar solution in that same supersaturated state.
tossups.r: A solution holding exactly as much solute as this property allows is called saturated. For 10 points, name this property, the maximum amount of solute that a solvent can hold.

tossups.p: Rules for this property in water say that nitrates and compounds of sodium, potassium, or ammonium almost always dissolve easily, while most carbonates and phosphates barely dissolve at all. Chemists use those rules to predict whether mixing two salt solutions will make a cloudy solid.
tossups.r: Such a solid, called a precipitate, forms when a compound can’t stay dissolved. For 10 points, name this property, which describes how much of a substance can dissolve in a solvent.

tossups.p: Silver nitrate is used to test for chloride ions, because silver chloride has such a low value of this property that a white solid appears. Rules for this property say that most chlorides dissolve in water, but the chlorides of silver, lead(II), and mercury(I) are exceptions.
tossups.r: Because so many substances have high values of this property in water, water is called the “universal solvent.” For 10 points, name this property that measures how much of a solute can dissolve.

tossups.p: Gray-black iodine crystals barely dissolve in water but dissolve readily in hexane, because iodine and hexane are both nonpolar. For a similar reason, dry cleaners remove greasy stains with nonpolar liquids instead of plain water.
tossups.r: This property follows the rule of thumb “like dissolves like.” For 10 points, name this property, which describes how much of a substance can dissolve in a solvent.

tossups.p: To dissolve an ionic solid, water must overcome its lattice energy, which holds the crystal together, and the hydration energy released as water molecules surround the freed ions helps pay that cost. In those surrounding shells, water molecules point their partially negative oxygen atoms toward the positive ions.
tossups.r: Water can surround ions because its molecules are polar. For 10 points, name this property, a measure of how much of a solute can dissolve in a solvent.

tossups.p: Liquids that mix together in any amounts, such as ethanol and water, are called miscible, meaning each has an unlimited value of this property in the other. Hexane and water are immiscible, so they separate into two layers when poured together.
tossups.r: Oil and water don’t mix because oil has a very low value of this property in water. For 10 points, name this property, which describes how well a substance dissolves.

tossups.p: Power plants that release warm water into rivers can harm fish, because this property of oxygen drops as the water warms up. That same drop explains why tiny bubbles of air appear on the inside of a pot of water long before the water boils.
tossups.r: Unlike gases, most solid solutes have higher values of this property in hot water. For 10 points, name this property, the most of a substance that can dissolve in a solvent.

tossups.p: Chemists purify a solid by recrystallization, dissolving it in a small amount of hot solvent and letting pure crystals form as the solution cools, while most impurities stay dissolved. That method works because this property usually rises with temperature.
tossups.r: On a graph of this property against temperature, points below the curve stand for unsaturated solutions. For 10 points, name this property, the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve.

tossups.p: A mixture of salt and sand can be separated by adding water, filtering out the sand, and then evaporating the water, because only the salt has a high value of this property in water. At room temperature, several times more sugar than table salt can dissolve in the same amount of water.
tossups.r: Adding solute past this property’s limit just leaves crystals at the bottom. For 10 points, name this property, a measure of how much of a solute can dissolve.

trap.title: The property, not its laws
trap.body: Tossups on this property are full of related answer lines: Henry’s law for gases, the solubility product K-sub-s-p for salts that barely dissolve, and saturated or supersaturated solutions. A player who hears “partial pressure” and blurts “Henry’s law,” or hears K-sub-s-p and says “solubility product,” loses the tossup when the question wants the property itself. Also remember that stirring and crushing change how fast something dissolves, not how much.
trap.fix: Listen for “this property” or “this quantity.” Answer with the property unless the question says “this law” (Henry’s law) or “this constant” (the solubility product).

topics.name: Redox
topics.kicker: Electron-transfer reactions · Oxidation is loss, reduction is gain
topics.dates: Lavoisier’s oxygen theory of burning, 1770s; Nernst equation, 1889
topics.briefing: When iron rusts, a battery powers your phone, or a campfire burns, electrons are moving from one substance to another. Chemists call these redox reactions, short for reduction–oxidation: the substance that loses electrons is oxidized, and the one that gains them is reduced. Students remember the pair with “OIL RIG”: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.
topics.answerHtml: Redox reactions (accept oxidation–reduction or reduction–oxidation reactions; prompt on oxidation or reduction alone)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Walther Nernst’s equation relates the voltage of a cell running one of these reactions to the concentrations of its reactants and products. Under standard conditions, that voltage equals the potential of the cathode’s half-reaction minus the potential of the anode’s half-reaction.
tossups.r: Batteries use these reactions to push electrons through a circuit. For 10 points, name these reactions that pair an oxidation with a reduction.

tossups.p: Chemists assign exactly zero volts to the standard hydrogen electrode, the reference point for ranking the half-reactions of these reactions. In typical textbook tables of that ranking, fluorine gas has the most positive standard electrode potential, while lithium has the most negative.
tossups.r: In these reactions, the substance that takes electrons is called the oxidizing agent. For 10 points, name these electron-transfer reactions.

tossups.p: In the thermite reaction, powdered aluminum pulls oxygen away from iron(III) oxide, releasing so much heat that the iron comes out molten and can weld railroad tracks together. In that reaction, aluminum gives up electrons while the iron ions take them.
tossups.r: Rusting is a much slower example of these reactions. For 10 points, name these reactions, remembered with the phrase “LEO the lion says GER.”

tossups.p: When hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen gas, some of its oxygen atoms gain electrons while others lose them, a special case called disproportionation. Chemists track such changes by giving each atom a charge-like number that rises when the atom loses electrons.
tossups.r: That number is called an oxidation state. For 10 points, name these reactions, summed up by the phrase “OIL RIG.”

tossups.p: To balance one of these reactions in acidic solution by the half-reaction method, chemists add water molecules to balance oxygen atoms and hydrogen ions to balance hydrogen atoms. The two halves are then multiplied so that the number of electrons given up equals the number taken in.
tossups.r: One half-reaction shows electrons being lost, and the other shows them being gained. For 10 points, name these electron-transfer reactions.

tossups.p: Purple permanganate ions turn nearly colorless when they take in electrons in acidic solution, so they act as their own indicator in titrations based on these reactions. Orange dichromate ions turn green when they are converted to chromium(III) ions in the same kind of reaction.
tossups.r: A substance that takes electrons from another is called an oxidizing agent. For 10 points, name these reactions that combine an oxidation with a reduction.

tossups.p: Blocks of zinc or magnesium are bolted to steel ship hulls so that they corrode in place of the steel, a method called cathodic protection. Galvanized nails are coated with zinc for the same reason.
tossups.r: Rusting, in which iron gives up electrons to oxygen, is an example of these reactions. For 10 points, name these electron-transfer reactions.

tossups.p: One half of these reactions takes its name from metalworking, where getting a metal out of its ore was called “reducing” the ore. The other half originally meant combining with oxygen, as when something burns.
tossups.r: Modern chemists define these reactions by the movement of electrons. For 10 points, name these reactions, remembered with the phrase “OIL RIG.”

tossups.p: When a strip of zinc is dipped into blue copper(II) sulfate solution, a reddish-brown coating of copper forms and the blue color fades, because zinc atoms hand electrons to the copper ions. The activity series ranks metals by how easily they give up electrons in reactions like this one.
tossups.r: In that reaction, zinc is the reducing agent. For 10 points, name these reactions in which electrons are transferred.

tossups.p: Tarnished silver can be cleaned by setting it on aluminum foil in hot water with baking soda, because the aluminum gives up electrons that turn black silver sulfide back into shiny silver. That black tarnish formed when the silver reacted with sulfur compounds in the air.
tossups.r: In these reactions, the substance that loses electrons is said to be oxidized. For 10 points, name these electron-transfer reactions.

tossups.p: In cellular respiration, the carrier molecule NAD⁺ picks up two electrons and a hydrogen ion to become NADH, and the electron transport chain finally hands electrons to oxygen. In photosynthesis, water gives up electrons and becomes oxygen gas.
tossups.r: Both processes are chains of these reactions, which pair a loss of electrons with a gain. For 10 points, name these reactions.

tossups.p: For one of these reactions, multiplying the number of electrons moved by Faraday’s constant and by the standard cell voltage gives the negative of the standard Gibbs free energy change. So a positive standard cell voltage means that the reaction happens on its own.
tossups.r: Galvanic cells, also called voltaic cells, use spontaneous examples of these reactions to make electricity. For 10 points, name these reactions.

tossups.p: The Hall–Héroult [“ay-ROO”] process makes aluminum by passing electricity through aluminum oxide dissolved in a molten mineral called cryolite, forcing one of these reactions that would never run on its own. Cells that need an outside power source like that are called electrolytic cells.
tossups.r: In every electrochemical cell, electrons are lost at the anode and gained at the cathode. For 10 points, name these reactions.

tossups.p: Under the bookkeeping rules for these reactions, an uncombined element such as solid copper is assigned zero, and fluorine in a compound is always assigned negative one. Oxygen is usually given negative two, though it is negative one in peroxides.
tossups.r: An atom’s oxidation number goes up when it loses electrons and down when it gains them. For 10 points, name these reactions.

tossups.p: Inside an alkaline battery, powdered zinc gives up electrons while manganese dioxide takes them in. A car’s lead-acid battery instead uses plates of lead and lead dioxide sitting in sulfuric acid.
tossups.r: Batteries turn the energy of these reactions into electricity. For 10 points, name these reactions in which electrons pass from one substance to another.

clues.t: Reactions in which electrons move from one substance to another
“OIL RIG”: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain
“LEO the lion says GER”: Lose Electrons, Oxidation; Gain Electrons, Reduction
Everyday examples: rusting, burning, and the reactions inside batteries
The oxidizing agent takes electrons and is reduced; the reducing agent gives up electrons and is oxidized
In electrochemical cells, oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode (“An Ox, Red Cat”)
Galvanic (voltaic) cells use spontaneous ones to make electricity; electrolytic cells use electricity to force them
An atom’s oxidation number rises when it loses electrons and falls when it gains them
Written as two half-reactions, balanced so the electrons lost equal the electrons gained
Rusting: iron gives up electrons to oxygen; galvanizing steel with a zinc coating protects it
Zinc dipped in blue copper(II) sulfate gets coated with copper as the blue fades; the activity series ranks metals by how easily they give up electrons
Cellular respiration and photosynthesis run on them; NAD⁺ picks up electrons to become NADH
Oxidation first meant combining with oxygen; reduction first meant getting a metal out of its ore
The Nernst equation relates a cell’s voltage to the concentrations of its reactants and products
Electrode potentials are measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, set at exactly 0 volts
In typical textbook tables, fluorine has the most positive standard electrode potential and lithium the most negative
ΔG° = −nFE°: Faraday’s constant links cell voltage to Gibbs free energy, so a positive voltage means the reaction is spontaneous
Thermite: aluminum takes oxygen from iron(III) oxide, making molten iron that can weld railroad tracks
Disproportionation: one element is both oxidized and reduced, as when hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen
Balancing in acid: add water to balance oxygen, H⁺ ions to balance hydrogen, then electrons to balance charge
Purple permanganate turns nearly colorless as it takes in electrons, so it is its own indicator in titrations
Orange dichromate turns green when it is converted to chromium(III) ions
Sacrificial blocks of zinc or magnesium on ship hulls corrode in place of the steel (cathodic protection)
The Hall–Héroult process makes aluminum by passing electricity through aluminum oxide dissolved in molten cryolite
Tarnished silver on aluminum foil in hot water with baking soda turns shiny again as the aluminum gives up electrons
Alkaline batteries: zinc gives up electrons and manganese dioxide takes them; car batteries use lead and lead dioxide
Bookkeeping rules: an uncombined element is assigned 0, fluorine in a compound is always −1, and oxygen is usually −2 (−1 in peroxides)

trap.title: Whole pair or one half?
trap.body: These reactions always pair two halves: oxidation, the loss of electrons, and reduction, the gain of electrons. Some tossups ask for just one half, so their answer is “reduction” or “oxidation” alone, not the whole pair. On a tossup about the whole pair, saying only one half earns a prompt, so be ready to say “redox” or “oxidation–reduction.”
trap.fix: Listen for what the question describes. “These reactions,” the Nernst equation, batteries, or “OIL RIG” mean the whole pair; a process of gaining electrons, happening at the cathode, or lowering an oxidation number means reduction, while losing electrons at the anode means oxidation.
trap.line: Real answer line: Redox reactions (accept oxidation–reduction or reduction–oxidation reactions; prompt on oxidation or reduction alone)

topics.name: Infrared spectroscopy
topics.kicker: Bonds vibrate in light just past red · Reveals a molecule’s functional groups
topics.dates: Infrared light discovered by William Herschel, 1800
topics.briefing: Shine infrared light, the invisible light just beyond red, through a sample, and its chemical bonds absorb certain wavelengths and start to stretch and bend like tiny springs. Infrared spectroscopy records which wavelengths get absorbed, producing a spectrum full of dips. Each kind of bond has its own signature, so chemists can quickly spot groups like an alcohol’s O–H or a carbonyl’s C=O, almost like reading a molecule’s barcode.
topics.answerHtml: Infrared spectroscopy (accept IR spectroscopy or FTIR; prompt on spectroscopy or vibrational spectroscopy)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A molecule’s vibration shows up in this technique only if it changes the molecule’s dipole moment, a selection rule that makes the stretch of a hydrogen molecule invisible to it. Raman spectroscopy, which detects light scattered by molecules, can pick up many of the vibrations that this technique misses.
tossups.r: This technique’s spectra plot how much light passes through a sample against wavenumber. For 10 points, name this technique that identifies functional groups using light just past the red end of the visible spectrum.

tossups.p: For molecules with a center of symmetry, the rule of mutual exclusion says that no vibration can appear both in Raman spectra and in this technique’s spectra. Carbon dioxide’s symmetric stretch is invisible to this technique, but its asymmetric stretch and its bending motion both show up.
tossups.r: In this technique, absorbed light makes chemical bonds stretch and bend. For 10 points, name this technique for identifying functional groups.

tossups.p: Modern instruments for this technique use a Michelson interferometer with a moving mirror and then apply a Fourier transform to turn the signal into a spectrum. Solid samples are often ground up with potassium bromide and pressed into a clear pellet, since that salt does not absorb this technique’s light.
tossups.r: The complicated region of its spectra below about 1500 reciprocal centimeters is called the fingerprint region. For 10 points, name this technique used to find a molecule’s functional groups.

tossups.p: William Coblentz pioneered this technique in the early 1900s by carefully recording the spectra of many organic compounds. The light it uses was discovered in 1800 by William Herschel, who saw a thermometer warm up when he placed it just past the red end of the spectrum made by a prism.
tossups.r: In this technique, a carbonyl group gives a strong, sharp peak near 1700 reciprocal centimeters. For 10 points, name this technique that measures how molecules absorb light just beyond red.

tossups.p: Treating each chemical bond as a spring that obeys Hooke’s law predicts where it will absorb in this technique: stiffer bonds and lighter atoms absorb at higher wavenumbers. That model explains why a carbon–carbon triple bond absorbs at a higher wavenumber than a carbon–carbon double bond.
tossups.r: This technique’s spectra are usually plotted against wavenumber, in reciprocal centimeters. For 10 points, name this technique that makes molecular bonds vibrate using light just past red.

tossups.p: Replacing a hydrogen atom with heavier deuterium lowers the wavenumber at which a bond absorbs in this technique, because the heavier atom vibrates more slowly. For the same reason, bonds to light hydrogen atoms, such as C–H, N–H, and O–H, absorb at the high-wavenumber end of its spectra.
tossups.r: Alcohols show a broad peak in this technique because of hydrogen bonding. For 10 points, name this technique that identifies functional groups.

tossups.p: The bending motions detected by this technique have names such as scissoring, rocking, wagging, and twisting. Bends usually absorb at lower wavenumbers than stretches of the same bonds, because bending a bond takes less energy than stretching it.
tossups.r: In this technique, an alcohol’s O–H group gives a broad peak near 3300. For 10 points, name this technique that uses light just past the red end of the visible spectrum.

tossups.p: A nonlinear molecule with N atoms can vibrate in 3N minus 6 ways, so water has three, a symmetric stretch, an asymmetric stretch, and a bend, and all three absorb in this technique. A linear molecule such as carbon dioxide has 3N minus 5 ways to vibrate instead.
tossups.r: In this technique’s spectra, the dips show light that was absorbed. For 10 points, name this technique that makes chemical bonds vibrate.

tossups.p: The same physics behind this technique explains the greenhouse effect, since carbon dioxide, water vapor, and methane absorb the heat radiation given off by Earth’s surface. Nitrogen and oxygen gas absorb almost none of it, because stretching their two identical atoms doesn’t change their dipole moment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique that identifies functional groups by measuring which light just past red makes their bonds stretch and bend.

tossups.p: In 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope used a version of this technique to detect carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of the exoplanet WASP-39b by studying starlight that filtered through the planet’s air. That gas showed up because its asymmetric stretch absorbs strongly.
tossups.r: On Earth, chemists use this technique to find functional groups such as carbonyls. For 10 points, name this technique that uses light just past red.

tossups.p: Liquid samples for this technique are often squeezed between polished plates of sodium chloride, which, unlike glass, let this technique’s light pass through. Water must be kept off those plates, both because it would dissolve them and because water itself absorbs this light strongly.
tossups.r: Below about 1500, its spectra have a complex fingerprint region unique to each compound. For 10 points, name this technique that makes molecular bonds stretch and bend.

tossups.p: Chemists can follow the conversion of an alcohol into a ketone with this technique by watching a broad peak near 3300 reciprocal centimeters disappear while a strong, sharp peak near 1700 appears. Those peaks come from the alcohol’s O–H group and the ketone’s C=O group.
tossups.r: Each functional group absorbs at its own typical wavenumbers in this technique. For 10 points, name this technique that identifies functional groups using light just past red.

tossups.p: In this technique, primary amines show two N–H peaks, from a symmetric and an asymmetric stretch, while secondary amines show only one. Tertiary amines show no N–H peak at all, because they have no hydrogen atoms bonded to their nitrogen.
tossups.r: This technique is a quick way to find a molecule’s functional groups. For 10 points, name this technique that makes chemical bonds vibrate.

tossups.p: The light used in this technique has too little energy to make electrons jump between energy levels, as ultraviolet and visible light can, but enough to change how molecules vibrate. Its spectra usually cover wavenumbers from 4000 down to 400 reciprocal centimeters.
tossups.r: Its spectra are read with wavenumber decreasing from left to right. For 10 points, name this technique that uses light just past red to find functional groups.

tossups.p: Forensic labs use this technique to identify paint chips and fibers by matching their spectra to reference libraries. Unlike nuclear magnetic resonance, which maps a molecule’s carbon and hydrogen atoms, this technique mainly reveals which functional groups are present.
tossups.r: Its spectra plot percent transmittance against wavenumber. For 10 points, name this technique that measures how molecules absorb light just beyond red.

clues.t: Identifies a molecule’s functional groups by measuring which light just past the red end of the visible spectrum it absorbs
Absorbed light makes chemical bonds vibrate by stretching and bending
A strong, sharp peak near 1700 reciprocal centimeters means a carbonyl (C=O) group
An alcohol’s O–H group gives a broad peak near 3300, widened by hydrogen bonding
Spectra plot percent transmittance against wavenumber, with dips where light was absorbed
Wavenumber is one over the wavelength, in reciprocal centimeters; most spectra run from 4000 down to 400
The fingerprint region, below about 1500 reciprocal centimeters, has a complex pattern unique to each compound
William Herschel discovered this kind of light in 1800 with a thermometer placed past the red end of a prism’s spectrum
Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide, water vapor, and methane absorb this kind of light; nitrogen and oxygen gas barely do
NMR maps carbon and hydrogen atoms and mass spectrometry weighs fragments, but this mainly reveals functional groups
Its light can’t make electrons jump between energy levels the way ultraviolet light can, but it changes how molecules vibrate
Turning an alcohol into a ketone makes the broad O–H peak vanish and a C=O peak near 1700 appear
Selection rule: a vibration absorbs only if it changes the molecule’s dipole moment
Carbon dioxide’s symmetric stretch doesn’t absorb, but its asymmetric stretch and bending do
Raman spectroscopy, which measures scattered light, is its partner; the rule of mutual exclusion applies to molecules with a center of symmetry
Fourier-transform instruments use a Michelson interferometer with a moving mirror
Samples go between sodium chloride plates or into potassium bromide pellets, because those salts, unlike glass, let this light through
William Coblentz pioneered it in the early 1900s by recording the spectra of many organic compounds
Bonds act like springs obeying Hooke’s law: stiffer bonds and lighter atoms absorb at higher wavenumbers, so triple bonds absorb higher than double bonds
Replacing hydrogen with heavier deuterium lowers a bond’s absorption wavenumber
A nonlinear molecule has 3N − 6 ways to vibrate (3N − 5 if linear); water has three
Primary amines show two N–H peaks, secondary amines one, and tertiary amines, with no N–H bond, none
Water is kept away from salt plates because it dissolves them and strongly absorbs this light itself
In 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope used it to find carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of the exoplanet WASP-39b
Bending motions have names like scissoring, rocking, wagging, and twisting; bends absorb at lower wavenumbers than stretches
Forensic labs identify paint chips and fibers by matching their spectra to reference libraries

trap.title: Technique, not the light
trap.body: Physics tossups sometimes ask for infrared radiation itself, the light William Herschel discovered, while chemistry tossups ask for this technique that uses it. Other spectroscopy answer lines are close cousins: NMR maps a molecule’s carbon and hydrogen atoms, mass spectrometry weighs its fragments, and Raman spectroscopy also measures vibrations, but by scattering light instead of absorbing it.
trap.fix: Wavenumbers, functional groups, bond stretching, and peaks near 1700 or 3300 mean this technique. Chemical shifts and magnetic fields mean NMR; mass-to-charge ratios mean mass spectrometry; scattered light points to Raman.
trap.line: Real answer line: Infrared spectroscopy (accept IR spectroscopy or FTIR; prompt on spectroscopy or vibrational spectroscopy)

topics.name: Lattice energy
topics.kicker: The grip that holds an ionic crystal together · Why table salt melts at 801 °C
topics.briefing: A grain of table salt is a tightly packed crystal of sodium and chloride ions, held together by the pull between opposite charges. Lattice energy measures that grip: the energy released when separated ions in a gas snap together into one mole of an ionic solid. Ions with bigger charges and smaller sizes grip harder, which is why magnesium oxide melts at over 2,800 °C while table salt melts at 801 °C.
topics.answerHtml: Lattice energy (accept lattice enthalpy; prompt on energy or enthalpy alone)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Magnesium oxide and calcium oxide have the same crystal structure as table salt, but this quantity is larger for magnesium oxide, because magnesium ions are smaller than calcium ions. This quantity can’t be measured directly in a laboratory, so chemists work it out from other energies.
tossups.r: The Born–Haber cycle uses Hess’s law to calculate it indirectly. For 10 points, name this energy released when gaseous ions come together to form one mole of an ionic solid.

tossups.p: Some instant hot packs warm up as calcium chloride dissolves, because the energy released as water surrounds its ions outweighs this quantity for that salt. Calcium chloride has a much larger value of this quantity than sodium chloride, partly because its calcium ions carry a +2 charge.
tossups.r: This quantity is larger for ions with bigger charges and smaller radii. For 10 points, name this measure of how strongly the ions in an ionic crystal are held together.

tossups.p: Magnesium oxide melts at over 2,800 degrees Celsius and is used to line furnaces, largely because this quantity is so large for magnesium oxide. Aluminum oxide, made of ions with charges of +3 and −2, has an even larger value of this quantity.
tossups.r: Because magnesium oxide’s ions carry double charges, its value is several times larger than table salt’s. For 10 points, name this energy that holds ionic crystals together.

tossups.p: To calculate this quantity for sodium chloride, chemists add up the energies of steps such as turning solid sodium into a gas, removing an electron from each sodium atom, splitting chlorine molecules into atoms, and adding an electron to each chlorine atom. Those steps form a cycle that also includes the compound’s enthalpy of formation.
tossups.r: That cycle, named for Max Born and Fritz Haber, relies on Hess’s law. For 10 points, name this energy released when gaseous ions form an ionic solid.

tossups.p: Sodium fluoride and calcium oxide are made of ions of nearly the same sizes, yet this quantity for calcium oxide is almost four times that for sodium fluoride, because the product of its ions’ charges is four times as large. That comparison shows how strongly ionic charge affects this quantity.
tossups.r: This quantity grows as ions get smaller and pack closer together. For 10 points, name this energy that holds an ionic solid together.

tossups.p: Among the alkali metal halides, lithium fluoride has the largest value of this quantity, while cesium iodide has the smallest. A fluoride has a larger value of this quantity than an iodide of the same metal, because fluoride ions are much smaller than iodide ions.
tossups.r: Smaller ions sit closer together, so they attract each other more strongly. For 10 points, name this energy released when gaseous ions form one mole of an ionic crystal.

tossups.p: Magnesium chloride is made of Mg²⁺ ions rather than Mg⁺ ions, because the much larger value of this quantity for doubly charged ions more than pays for removing magnesium’s second electron. Sodium does not form Na²⁺ ions, since removing a second electron from sodium would cost far more energy than this quantity could repay.
tossups.r: This quantity grows with the product of the ions’ charges. For 10 points, name this energy that holds ionic compounds together.

tossups.p: Instant cold packs get cold when ammonium nitrate dissolves in water, because the energy needed to overcome this quantity for that salt is larger than the energy released when water molecules surround its ions. Whether dissolving a salt takes in or gives off heat depends on a contest between this quantity and that hydration energy.
tossups.r: Ionic compounds with large values of this quantity tend to have high melting points. For 10 points, name this energy released when gaseous ions form an ionic solid.

tossups.p: In a sodium chloride crystal, each ion is surrounded by six ions of the opposite charge, while in cesium chloride each ion has eight such neighbors, which changes the geometric factor used to calculate this quantity. This quantity adds up the attractions and repulsions among all the ions in a crystal, not just neighboring pairs.
tossups.r: Like Coulomb’s law, this quantity grows with the ions’ charges and shrinks as they get farther apart. For 10 points, name this energy that holds an ionic crystal together.

tossups.p: British textbooks often split this quantity into a negative “formation” version, for gaseous ions coming together, and a positive “dissociation” version, for a crystal being pulled apart into gaseous ions. Both versions have the same size, usually given in kilojoules per mole.
tossups.r: Forming an ionic solid from gaseous ions releases energy. For 10 points, name this quantity, the energy released when gaseous ions form one mole of an ionic solid.

tossups.p: Melting points fall from sodium fluoride to sodium chloride to sodium bromide to sodium iodide, because this quantity shrinks as the halide ion gets bigger. Sodium chloride itself must be heated to 801 degrees Celsius before it melts.
tossups.r: This quantity is greater for smaller ions with larger charges. For 10 points, name this energy that holds the ions of a salt crystal together.

tossups.p: Removing an electron from a sodium atom takes more energy than a chlorine atom gives off when it gains one, so making separate sodium and chloride ions costs energy overall. Sodium chloride still forms readily, because this quantity releases far more energy when those ions pack into a crystal.
tossups.r: This quantity is one step in the Born–Haber cycle. For 10 points, name this energy released when gaseous ions form an ionic solid.

tossups.p: Max Born, who later won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Physics, and Fritz Haber, who won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for making ammonia, devised a 1919 cycle for calculating this quantity. Their cycle is needed because this quantity cannot be measured directly.
tossups.r: This quantity is much larger for magnesium oxide than for sodium chloride. For 10 points, name this energy that holds ionic crystals together.

tossups.p: Potassium chloride has a smaller value of this quantity than sodium chloride, because potassium ions are larger and sit farther from the chloride ions. Moving down group 1, the chlorides’ values of this quantity fall from lithium chloride to cesium chloride.
tossups.r: This quantity is greater when ions have larger charges. For 10 points, name this energy released when gaseous ions form one mole of an ionic solid.

tossups.p: Adding a second electron to an oxygen atom takes energy instead of releasing it, yet magnesium oxide still forms readily, because this quantity is so large for its doubly charged ions. This quantity for magnesium oxide is nearly five times the value for sodium chloride.
tossups.r: This quantity depends on the charges and sizes of the ions. For 10 points, name this energy that holds an ionic crystal together.

clues.t: The energy released when gaseous ions come together to form one mole of an ionic solid
Equivalently, the energy needed to pull one mole of an ionic solid apart into gaseous ions
Larger for ions with bigger charges and smaller sizes
Magnesium oxide (+2 and −2 ions) has a value nearly five times that of sodium chloride (+1 and −1 ions)
Can’t be measured directly, so it is found indirectly with the Born–Haber cycle, which uses Hess’s law
Follows Coulomb’s law: grows with the product of the ions’ charges and shrinks as the ions get farther apart
Higher values mean higher melting points; melting points fall from sodium fluoride to sodium iodide
Among the alkali metal halides, lithium fluoride has the largest value and cesium iodide the smallest
Dissolving a salt means overcoming this energy; the hydration energy released as water surrounds the ions helps pay for it
Ammonium nitrate cold packs get cold because pulling the crystal apart takes more energy than hydration gives back
Born–Haber steps for sodium chloride: vaporize sodium, remove its electron, split chlorine molecules, add electrons to chlorine, then form the solid
Making separate Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions costs energy overall, but forming the crystal releases far more, so sodium chloride forms readily
Potassium chloride’s value is smaller than sodium chloride’s because potassium ions are larger
Magnesium oxide’s value is larger than calcium oxide’s because magnesium ions are smaller; both have table salt’s crystal structure
Calcium chloride hot packs warm up because the energy released as water surrounds the ions outweighs the energy holding the crystal together
Sodium fluoride and calcium oxide have ions of nearly equal size, but calcium oxide’s value is almost four times as large because both of its ions carry double charges
In sodium chloride each ion has six neighbors of opposite charge; in cesium chloride each has eight
Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ because the bigger value for doubly charged ions pays for its second electron; sodium doesn’t form Na²⁺ because its second electron costs far too much
Adding a second electron to oxygen takes energy, yet magnesium oxide forms readily because this energy is so large
Max Born (1954 Nobel Prize in Physics) and Fritz Haber (1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry) devised their cycle in 1919
British textbooks use a negative “formation” version and a positive “dissociation” version, both in kilojoules per mole
Magnesium oxide melts at over 2,800 °C and lines furnaces; aluminum oxide’s +3 ions give an even larger value
It adds up the attractions and repulsions among all the ions in a crystal, not just neighboring pairs
Down group 1, the chlorides’ values fall from lithium chloride to cesium chloride

trap.title: Which energy is it?
trap.body: Tossups on this quantity are crowded with other energies: the metal’s ionization energy, the nonmetal’s electron affinity, the bond energy of molecules like Cl₂, and the hydration energy of dissolving ions. Each of those is only one step in the Born–Haber cycle or one side of a comparison, and naming one of them loses the tossup. Saying just “energy” or “enthalpy” earns a prompt.
trap.fix: If the clues describe gaseous ions coming together into a crystal, the Born–Haber cycle, or the charges and melting points of salts, answer with this quantity. The energy to pull an electron off a single gaseous atom is ionization energy instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: Lattice energy (accept lattice enthalpy; prompt on energy or enthalpy alone)

topics.name: Titanium
topics.kicker: Element 22, strong as steel but far lighter · Named for the Titans
topics.briefing: Titanium is a silvery metal as strong as many steels but only a little more than half as dense, which makes it perfect for jet engines, spacecraft, and racing bikes. A thin coat of oxide keeps it from corroding, and the body tolerates it well, so it is a top choice for artificial hips and dental implants. Its white dioxide brightens paint, toothpaste, and sunscreen, and the element itself is named for the Titans of Greek myth.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: William Gregor, a clergyman in Cornwall, England, found this element in 1791 in a black sand that also contained iron. Martin Heinrich Klaproth [“KLAHP-roht”] found it again in the mineral rutile and gave it its name in 1795.
tossups.r: Klaproth named it for the Titans of Greek mythology. For 10 points, name this transition metal with atomic number 22.

tossups.p: In the Kroll process, this element’s tetrachloride is heated with molten magnesium, producing a porous form of the metal called “sponge.” That process, developed by William Kroll around 1940, became the main way to make this metal.
tossups.r: Strong, light alloys of this metal are used in jet engines and airplane frames. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 22.

tossups.p: A colorless liquid compound of this element, nicknamed “tickle,” fumes in moist air to form thick white clouds, so it has been used to make smoke screens and skywriting. That compound, a tetrachloride, is also the starting material for making the pure metal.
tossups.r: This element’s white dioxide is used in paint and sunscreen. For 10 points, name this metal named for the Titans.

tossups.p: Karl Ziegler and Giulio Natta shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for catalysts made from chlorides of this element and aluminum compounds, which link small molecules into plastics such as polypropylene. This metal’s most common alloy contains 6 percent aluminum and 4 percent vanadium.
tossups.r: It sits just above zirconium on the periodic table. For 10 points, name this group 4 transition metal with atomic number 22.

tossups.p: The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird spy plane was built mostly from this metal, some of it from supplies secretly bought from the Soviet Union, because aluminum would have weakened in the heat of flying more than three times the speed of sound.
tossups.r: Golf clubs and bicycle frames are also made of this light, strong metal. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 22.

tossups.p: Per-Ingvar Brånemark [“BROH-neh-mark”] discovered that living bone grows tightly onto this metal, a process he named osseointegration [“OSS-ee-oh-in-teh-GRAY-shun”], which led to modern dental implants. A thin layer of oxide keeps this metal from corroding inside the body.
tossups.r: Artificial hips and knees are often made of it. For 10 points, name this strong, light element with atomic number 22.

tossups.p: In 1972, Akira Fujishima and Kenichi Honda shone ultraviolet light on an electrode made of this element’s dioxide to split water, launching research into the kind of photocatalysts used in self-cleaning windows.
tossups.r: That white dioxide also blocks ultraviolet light in many sunscreens. For 10 points, name this metal named for the Titans of Greek myth.

tossups.p: Nitinol, a “shape-memory” alloy that springs back to its original shape when warmed, combines nickel with this element, and its name comes partly from the Naval Ordnance Laboratory where it was developed. Thin, springy nitinol wires are used in dental braces and medical stents.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 22, a light, strong transition metal named for the Titans.

tossups.p: This element is mined mainly from the minerals ilmenite [“ILL-meh-nite”], which also contains iron, and rutile [“ROO-teel”], which is this element’s dioxide. It is the ninth most abundant element in Earth’s crust.
tossups.r: A thin oxide layer protects this metal from corrosion. For 10 points, name this transition metal with atomic number 22.

tossups.p: A hard, gold-colored nitride of this element coats drill bits and other cutting tools so they last longer. This element’s most stable compounds have it in the +4 oxidation state, as in its dioxide.
tossups.r: This metal sits between scandium and vanadium on the periodic table. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 22.

tossups.p: Matthew Hunter of Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute first made this metal in a nearly pure form in 1910 by heating its tetrachloride with sodium. Pure samples of this metal are hard to make because, when hot, it reacts with both the oxygen and the nitrogen in air.
tossups.r: This metal’s alloys are as strong as many steels but much less dense. For 10 points, name this element named for the Titans.

tossups.p: The Soviet Union built its fast Alfa-class submarines with hulls made of this metal’s alloys, which are strong, light, and resist corrosion by seawater. This element sits above zirconium and hafnium in group 4 of the periodic table.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this light, strong metal with atomic number 22, named for the Titans of Greek myth.

tossups.p: Frank Gehry’s Guggenheim Museum Bilbao [“bil-BAH-oh”] in Spain is covered with thousands of thin, shiny panels of this metal. This metal is also used for eyeglass frames and watches because it is light and does not corrode easily.
tossups.r: Its white dioxide is the pigment in many paints. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 22.

tossups.p: In the 1900s, artists began replacing poisonous lead white with a white paint made from this element’s dioxide. That dioxide became the most widely used white pigment, found in house paint, paper, and toothpaste.
tossups.r: It also blocks ultraviolet light in mineral sunscreens. For 10 points, name this metal named for the Titans.

tossups.p: This metal has a density of about 4.5 grams per cubic centimeter, only a little more than half that of steel, yet its alloys can be just as strong. Its melting point, about 1,670 degrees Celsius, is higher than iron’s.
tossups.r: Jet engines, spacecraft, and racing bikes use this light, strong metal. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 22.

trap.title: Element, not its compound
trap.body: Many clues for this element are really about its compounds: the white dioxide in paint and sunscreen, the fuming tetrachloride nicknamed “tickle,” and the gold-colored nitride on drill bits. Answering with a compound, such as “titanium dioxide,” is wrong when the question asks for the element. The element’s name comes from the Titans, but Saturn’s moon Titan and the mythological Titans are separate answer lines.
trap.fix: Listen for “this element” or “this metal” and give just the element’s name. Only answer with a compound if the question says “this compound” or “this pigment.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Titanium (accept Ti; do not accept “titanium dioxide”)

topics.name: Boyle’s law
topics.kicker: Squeeze a gas and its pressure rises · PV stays constant at fixed temperature
topics.briefing: Push a syringe’s plunger while blocking its tip, and the trapped air pushes back harder the more you squeeze it. Robert Boyle measured this in 1662: at a constant temperature, a gas’s pressure and volume are inversely proportional, so halving the volume doubles the pressure. Written PV = k, Boyle’s law explains why your lungs fill when your diaphragm moves down and why a sealed bag of chips puffs up on a mountaintop.
topics.answerHtml: Boyle’s law (accept Boyle–Mariotte law or Mariotte’s law; prompt on Boyle alone)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Richard Towneley and Henry Power noticed this relationship in the early 1660s, before its namesake confirmed it with careful measurements. Its namesake published it in 1662, in a defense of his work against the Jesuit critic Franciscus Linus.
tossups.r: Doubling the pressure on a gas obeying this law halves its volume. For 10 points, name this law that relates a gas’s pressure and volume at constant temperature.

tossups.p: A French physicist who also discovered the blind spot in the human eye found this law on his own in 1676, so in France it is often called by his name. This law describes an isothermal process, one in which the temperature stays the same.
tossups.r: It says that a gas’s pressure times its volume stays constant. For 10 points, name this gas law named for an Irish-born chemist of the 1600s.

tossups.p: At a temperature named for this law’s namesake, a real gas obeys this law over a wide range of pressures, because the effects of its molecules’ attractions and their sizes cancel out. Real gases break this law at very high pressures.
tossups.r: This law says that halving a gas’s volume doubles its pressure if the temperature stays fixed. For 10 points, name this law relating pressure and volume.

tossups.p: In his 1738 book _Hydrodynamica_, Daniel Bernoulli derived this law by imagining gas particles bouncing off the walls of their container. In the kinetic theory of gases, this law holds because squeezing a gas into a smaller space makes its particles hit the walls more often.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law which states that, at constant temperature, the pressure of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume.

tossups.p: Plotting a gas’s pressure against one over its volume gives a straight line through the origin for a gas obeying this law, while plotting pressure against volume gives a curve called a hyperbola. Each such curve, drawn for one temperature, is called an isotherm.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas law summed up by saying that pressure times volume stays the same.

tossups.p: Robert Hooke built the air pump that this law’s namesake used in his experiments on air, and a law about springs is named for Hooke. Breathing follows this law: when the diaphragm moves down, the chest cavity gets bigger, so the pressure inside the lungs drops.
tossups.r: Air then rushes in to fill the lungs. For 10 points, name this law relating a gas’s pressure and volume.

tossups.p: A balloon filled with air 10 meters underwater roughly doubles in volume by the time it reaches the surface, because the pressure at that depth is about twice the pressure at the surface. Weather balloons swell as they rise for a similar reason, since the air pressure around them keeps falling.
tossups.r: Scuba divers are taught never to hold their breath while rising. For 10 points, name this law relating a gas’s pressure and volume.

tossups.p: A marshmallow sealed inside a syringe swells up when the plunger is pulled back, because lowering the pressure lets the tiny pockets of air inside it expand. A sealed bag of chips puffs up at high altitude for the same reason.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law stating that a gas’s volume rises as its pressure falls, if its temperature stays constant.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake was born at Lismore Castle in Ireland, a son of the Earl of Cork. He wrote _The Sceptical Chymist_ in 1661 and helped found the Royal Society.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law which says that a gas’s pressure and volume are inversely proportional at constant temperature.

tossups.p: Thomas Hobbes, the author of _Leviathan_, attacked the air-pump experiments that this law’s namesake used to study air. This law can be joined with Charles’s law and Gay-Lussac’s law to form the combined gas law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law which says that squeezing a gas into a smaller space raises its pressure, as long as its temperature stays the same.

tossups.p: If a gas obeying this law at 1 atmosphere is squeezed from 6 liters down to 2 liters, its pressure rises to 3 atmospheres. This law works only when both the temperature and the amount of gas stay fixed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas law often written as P-one V-one equals P-two V-two.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake described the “spring of the air,” its push back against being squeezed, in a 1660 book of experiments made with an air pump. For a later edition, he trapped air in the sealed short arm of a J-shaped tube and compressed it by pouring mercury into the long arm.
tossups.r: This law says that a gas’s pressure rises as its volume shrinks. For 10 points, name this law relating the pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature.

tossups.p: For a gas that perfectly obeys this law, a graph of pressure times volume against pressure is a flat, horizontal line. Real gases curve away from that line at high pressures, because their molecules take up space and attract one another.
tossups.r: This law says that pressure and volume are inversely proportional. For 10 points, name this gas law that holds at constant temperature.

tossups.p: Squeezing a sealed plastic bottle makes a small toy called a Cartesian diver sink, because the higher pressure shrinks the air bubble trapped inside the diver. Letting go lets the bubble expand again, so the diver floats back up.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law stating that, at constant temperature, a gas’s volume shrinks as the pressure on it rises.

tossups.p: Émile Clapeyron [“klah-pay-RAWN”] combined this law with Charles’s law in 1834 to state the ideal gas law. Real gases follow this law best at low pressures and high temperatures, where their molecules are far apart and barely attract one another.
tossups.r: At constant temperature, the ideal gas law reduces to this law. For 10 points, name this law relating a gas’s pressure and volume.

Pressure times volume stays constant: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂
Double the pressure on a gas and its volume is cut in half

Describes an isothermal process: the temperature and the amount of gas stay fixed
Kinetic theory: in a smaller space, gas particles hit the walls more often, so the pressure rises
Breathing: the diaphragm moves down, the chest gets bigger, the pressure in the lungs drops, and air flows in
Pulling back a syringe’s plunger makes more room, lowering the pressure so liquid is drawn in

A sealed bag of chips puffs up at high altitude; a marshmallow in a syringe swells when the plunger is pulled back
Joined with Charles’s and Gay-Lussac’s laws in the combined gas law; the ideal gas law reduces to it at constant temperature
Pressure plotted against volume is a curve called a hyperbola; pressure against one over volume is a straight line
Squeezing a bottle makes a Cartesian diver sink by shrinking its air bubble
Richard Towneley and Henry Power noticed the relationship first, in the early 1660s
Its namesake published it in 1662, defending his work against the Jesuit critic Franciscus Linus
His 1660 book of air-pump experiments described the “spring of the air”
Its namesake poured mercury into a J-shaped tube to squeeze a pocket of trapped air
Robert Hooke, for whom a law about springs is named, built the air pump
Edme Mariotte, who also discovered the eye’s blind spot, found it independently in 1676
At a temperature named for its namesake, a real gas obeys it over a wide range of pressures
