Pressure times volume plotted against pressure is a flat line for an ideal gas; real gases curve away at high pressure
Its namesake wrote _The Sceptical Chymist_ (1661) and helped found the Royal Society
Its namesake was born at Lismore Castle in Ireland, a son of the Earl of Cork
Thomas Hobbes, author of _Leviathan_, attacked its namesake’s air-pump experiments
Émile Clapeyron combined it with Charles’s law in 1834 to state the ideal gas law

trap.title: Pressure and volume only
trap.body: Gas-law tossups blur together: Charles’s law links volume and temperature, Gay-Lussac’s law links pressure and temperature, and the ideal gas law ties everything together as PV = nRT. This law is the one where the temperature stays fixed while pressure and volume trade off. Hearing “Robert Hooke” in an early clue can also lure a wrong buzz of “Hooke’s law,” which is about springs.
trap.fix: Ask which quantity is held constant. Constant temperature, with pressure and volume moving in opposite directions, means this law; constant pressure means Charles’s law; constant volume means Gay-Lussac’s law. Saying just “Boyle” earns a prompt, so add “law.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Boyle’s law (accept Boyle–Mariotte law or Mariotte’s law; prompt on Boyle alone)

topics.name: Atomic orbitals
topics.kicker: Where an atom’s electrons are likely to be · Labeled s, p, d, and f
topics.briefing: Electrons don’t circle the nucleus like tiny planets. Instead, quantum mechanics says each electron lives in an atomic orbital, a fuzzy cloud-shaped region where it is most likely to be found, and each orbital can hold at most two electrons. Orbitals come in shapes labeled s (a sphere), p (a dumbbell), d (mostly four-leaf clovers), and f, and the order in which they fill gives the periodic table its shape.
topics.answerHtml: Atomic orbitals (accept orbitals or electron orbitals; accept specific types such as s orbitals or p orbitals; prompt on electron clouds or wave functions; do not accept “orbits,” “shells,” or “molecular orbitals”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Robert Mulliken coined the name for these regions in 1932. Linus Pauling showed that they can mix to form hybrids, such as the four sp³ hybrids that point to the corners of a tetrahedron around the carbon atom in methane.
tossups.r: Each of these regions can hold at most two electrons. For 10 points, name these regions labeled s, p, d, and f.

tossups.p: The letters naming the first four kinds of these regions come from old descriptions of lines in atomic spectra: sharp, principal, diffuse, and fundamental. The second kind comes in sets of three that point along the x, y, and z axes.
tossups.r: The first kind is shaped like a sphere. For 10 points, name these regions where an atom’s electrons are most likely to be found.

tossups.p: The number of radial nodes in one of these regions equals n minus l minus 1, so the 2s version has one spherical node where the electron is never found. The number of angular nodes in one of these regions equals its quantum number l.
tossups.r: Each of these regions holds at most two electrons. For 10 points, name these regions around a nucleus, labeled s, p, d, and f.

tossups.p: The magnetic quantum number tells how one of these regions is oriented in space, and it can take any whole-number value from negative l to positive l. As a result, a subshell with quantum number l contains 2l plus 1 of these regions.
tossups.r: That gives one s, three p, five d, and seven f of them. For 10 points, name these regions, each holding up to two electrons, where electrons are likely to be found.

tossups.p: Hund’s rule says that electrons spread out one at a time into these regions when the regions have equal energy, all with parallel spins, before any electrons pair up. The Aufbau [“OWF-bow”] principle says that these regions fill from lowest energy to highest.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these regions of an atom, labeled s, p, d, and f, that each hold up to two electrons.

tossups.p: Chromium and copper break the usual filling order by moving an electron out of the 4s one of these regions and into the 3d set, which then becomes exactly half full for chromium and completely full for copper.
tossups.r: Diagrams of boxes and arrows show how electrons fill these regions. For 10 points, name these regions around a nucleus, labeled s, p, d, and f.

tossups.p: Four of the five 3d versions of these regions have four lobes, like a four-leaf clover, while the fifth, called d z-squared, has two lobes with a doughnut-shaped ring around its middle. The seven f versions have even more complicated shapes.
tossups.r: The p versions are shaped like dumbbells, and the s versions are spheres. For 10 points, name these regions where electrons are most likely to be found.

tossups.p: Solving Erwin Schrödinger’s [“SHROH-ding-er”] equation for the hydrogen atom gives these regions as wave functions, and Max Born proposed that squaring a wave function gives the probability of finding an electron. Unlike the circular paths in Niels Bohr’s model, these regions do not give an electron’s exact path.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these regions of space, labeled s, p, d, and f, where electrons are most likely to be found.

tossups.p: For hydrogen’s lowest-energy one of these regions, the most likely distance between the electron and the nucleus equals the Bohr radius, about 53 picometers. That region, called 1s, is perfectly spherical.
tossups.r: Each of these regions holds at most two electrons. For 10 points, name these regions where an electron is most likely to be found.

tossups.p: In atoms with many electrons, the 2s one of these regions has a lower energy than the 2p ones, because s electrons spend more time close to the nucleus and are shielded less. In the simple model of a hydrogen atom, though, the 2s and 2p ones have the same energy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these regions, which come in s, p, d, and f types, where an atom’s electrons are found.

tossups.p: A g type of these regions, with an angular momentum quantum number of 4, is not filled in the ground state of any known element. Mathematical functions called spherical harmonics describe the angular shapes of these regions in a hydrogen atom.
tossups.r: The periodic table’s s, p, d, and f blocks are named for them. For 10 points, name these regions where electrons are most likely to be found around a nucleus.

tossups.p: A sigma bond forms when two of these regions overlap head-on, while a pi bond forms when two p versions of these regions overlap side by side. A double bond contains one sigma bond and one pi bond.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these regions of an atom, labeled s, p, d, and f, that can each hold two electrons.

tossups.p: In an isolated atom, the three 2p versions of these regions have the same energy, so they are called degenerate. A magnetic field splits those energies apart, which divides a single spectral line into several lines in the Zeeman effect.
tossups.r: Wolfgang Pauli’s exclusion principle limits each of these regions to two electrons with opposite spins. For 10 points, name these regions labeled s, p, d, and f.

tossups.p: The shell with principal quantum number n contains n squared of these regions, so it can hold up to 2n squared electrons. The third shell therefore has nine of these regions: one 3s, three 3p, and five 3d.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these regions around a nucleus where electrons are most likely to be found.

tossups.p: The two lobes of a p version of these regions have opposite phases, separated by a flat nodal plane through the nucleus where the electron is never found. Chemists often draw the lobes in two colors to show those phases, which matter when the regions overlap to form bonds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these regions of an atom, labeled s, p, d, and f, that each hold up to two electrons.

clues.t: Regions around a nucleus where an electron is most likely to be found
Each holds at most two electrons, which must have opposite spins (Pauli exclusion principle)
Labeled s, p, d, and f
The s type is a sphere, and the p type is shaped like a dumbbell
A subshell has one s, three p, five d, or seven f of them (2l + 1)
Quantum numbers: n sets size and energy, l sets shape, and the magnetic number sets orientation
Aufbau principle: they fill from lowest energy to highest, so 4s fills before 3d
Hund’s rule: electrons enter equal-energy ones singly, with parallel spins, before pairing up
Replaced the fixed circular paths of Niels Bohr’s model with clouds of probability
Four of the five d ones look like four-leaf clovers; d z-squared has two lobes and a doughnut-shaped ring
The periodic table’s s, p, d, and f blocks are named for them; the lanthanides and actinides fill the f type
They are wave functions from Schrödinger’s equation; squaring one gives the probability of finding the electron (Max Born)
Box-and-arrow diagrams show how electrons fill them
The letters come from old names for spectral lines: sharp, principal, diffuse, and fundamental
Robert Mulliken coined their name in 1932
Linus Pauling showed they mix into hybrids: one s and three p make four sp³ hybrids, as in methane
Radial nodes = n − l − 1 and angular nodes = l, so the 2s has one spherical node
A p type’s two lobes have opposite phases, split by a nodal plane through the nucleus
The magnetic quantum number runs from −l to +l, giving 2l + 1 orientations
Shell n contains n squared of them and up to 2n squared electrons, so the third shell has nine
Chromium and copper move an electron from 4s into 3d, making the 3d set half full or completely full
For hydrogen’s 1s, the most likely distance between electron and nucleus is the Bohr radius, about 53 picometers
In many-electron atoms, 2s is lower in energy than 2p because s electrons get closer to the nucleus and are shielded less; in simple hydrogen they are equal
Spherical harmonics describe their angular shapes in a hydrogen atom
The g type (l = 4) is not filled in the ground state of any known element
Ones with equal energy, like the three 2p, are degenerate; a magnetic field splits them (the Zeeman effect)
Head-on overlap makes a sigma bond; side-by-side overlap of two p types makes a pi bond

trap.title: Not orbits, not shells
trap.body: Niels Bohr’s older model put electrons on circular orbits, so answering “orbits” for these modern probability regions is wrong. Shells (energy levels, numbered n) and subshells (sets like 2p) are different answers too: a shell holds many of these regions, and each region holds at most two electrons. Molecular orbitals, which spread across a whole molecule, and hybrid orbitals such as sp³ are separate answer lines.
trap.fix: If the clues say “at most two electrons,” spheres and dumbbells, nodes, or the magnetic quantum number, answer with this term. Circular paths and Bohr mean orbits; numbered energy levels mean shells; regions spread over several bonded atoms mean molecular orbitals.
trap.line: Real answer line: Atomic orbitals (accept orbitals or electron orbitals; accept specific types such as s orbitals or p orbitals; prompt on electron clouds or wave functions; do not accept “orbits,” “shells,” or “molecular orbitals”)

topics.name: Chemical equilibrium
topics.kicker: Forward and reverse reactions in balance · Le Chatelier predicts how it shifts
topics.dates: Law of mass action, 1864; Le Chatelier’s principle, 1884
topics.briefing: Inside a sealed tube of brown nitrogen dioxide gas, molecules keep pairing up into colorless dinitrogen tetroxide and splitting apart again at exactly the same rate, so the color never changes. That balance is chemical equilibrium: the forward and reverse reactions run at equal speeds, so the amounts of reactants and products stay steady even though both reactions keep going. Disturb it by heating, squeezing, or adding chemicals, and it shifts to undo the change, as Le Chatelier’s principle predicts.
topics.answerHtml: Chemical equilibrium (accept dynamic equilibrium or equilibria; prompt on equilibrium constant or thermodynamic equilibrium; do not accept “Le Chatelier’s principle”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: While traveling in Egypt with Napoleon’s expedition, Claude Louis Berthollet [“bair-toh-LAY”] noticed sodium carbonate forming around salt lakes, a sign that a reaction’s direction can depend on how much of each substance is present. That idea paved the way for the modern understanding of this state.
tossups.r: At this state, the forward and reverse reactions run at the same rate. For 10 points, name this balanced state of a reversible reaction.

tossups.p: In 1864, the Norwegians Cato Guldberg and Peter Waage [“VAW-geh”] stated the law of mass action, which gives the constant K for this state as product concentrations over reactant concentrations, each raised to the power of its coefficient. Pure solids and liquids are left out of that ratio.
tossups.r: Once a reaction reaches this state, its concentrations stop changing. For 10 points, name this state in which forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.

tossups.p: The van ’t Hoff [“vahnt HOFF”] equation shows how the constant for this state changes with temperature, depending on the reaction’s standard enthalpy change. Heating a reaction that gives off heat shifts this state back toward the reactants.
tossups.r: Le Chatelier’s principle predicts how this state shifts when it is disturbed. For 10 points, name this state of a reversible reaction in which concentrations stay constant.

tossups.p: At this state, the Gibbs free energy change for a reaction is zero, and the standard Gibbs free energy change equals negative RT times the natural log of this state’s constant. A constant greater than 1 means that products are favored.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state in which a reversible reaction’s forward and reverse rates are equal.

tossups.p: If a reaction’s quotient Q is smaller than its constant K, the reaction moves forward, making more products, until Q equals K. If Q is larger than K, the reaction runs backward instead, turning products back into reactants.
tossups.r: ICE tables, whose E stands for this state, help solve problems about it. For 10 points, name this state in which the amounts of reactants and products stay constant.

tossups.p: Sealed tubes of brown nitrogen dioxide fade when chilled in ice water, as more of the gas pairs up into colorless dinitrogen tetroxide, and they turn darker brown when heated. That color change shows that the pairing-up reaction gives off heat.
tossups.r: Such tubes show how this state shifts when it is disturbed. For 10 points, name this state in which a reaction’s forward and reverse rates are equal.

tossups.p: Paper soaked in cobalt(II) chloride turns pink in humid air and blue when dry, and heating a pink solution of cobalt chloride in hydrochloric acid turns it blue. Cooling that solution turns it pink again.
tossups.r: Those color changes show this state shifting to undo a stress, as Le Chatelier’s principle predicts. For 10 points, name this state of a reversible reaction.

tossups.p: In the Haber process, high pressure pushes this state toward ammonia, because the product side has fewer moles of gas, while an iron catalyst helps the reaction reach this state faster without changing where it lies. A lower temperature would give more ammonia but make the reaction far too slow.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this balanced state of a reversible reaction, which is shown with a double arrow.

tossups.p: Adding helium to a sealed, rigid container of reacting gases at this state does not shift it, because the partial pressures of the reacting gases stay the same. Squeezing the container into a smaller volume, however, shifts this state toward the side with fewer gas molecules.
tossups.r: Le Chatelier’s principle says this state shifts to relieve any stress. For 10 points, name this state in which forward and reverse reactions happen at equal rates.

tossups.p: Adding more thiocyanate [“thy-oh-SY-uh-nate”] ions to a pale solution of iron(III) ions turns it a deeper red, as this state shifts toward the red complex that the two ions form. Removing iron(III) ions would make the color fade instead.
tossups.r: Adding a reactant shifts this state toward the products. For 10 points, name this state of a reversible reaction.

tossups.p: For reactions of gases, the constant for this state can be written with partial pressures as K-sub-p, which equals K-sub-c times RT raised to the change in moles of gas. Pure solids, such as the carbon in the reaction of carbon with steam, are left out of either constant.
tossups.r: Only a change in temperature alters the value of this state’s constant. For 10 points, name this state in which the concentrations of reactants and products stop changing.

tossups.p: Pure water at 25 degrees Celsius reaches this state with its hydrogen and hydroxide ions, giving a constant, K-sub-w, of 1.0 times 10 to the minus 14. Weak acids reach this state in water with only a small fraction of their molecules split into ions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse rates match.

tossups.p: The principle of detailed balance says that at this state, every individual step of a reaction’s mechanism runs forward and backward at equal rates. A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so it helps a system reach this state faster but doesn’t change where it lies.
tossups.r: Both reactions keep running at this state, so it is called dynamic. For 10 points, name this state, shown with a double arrow, in which concentrations stay constant.

tossups.p: In the contact process for making sulfuric acid, sulfur dioxide and oxygen react over a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst to reach this state with sulfur trioxide. Because the forward reaction gives off heat, raising the temperature shifts this state back toward the reactants.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse rates are equal.

tossups.p: A saturated solution of silver chloride sits at this state with the undissolved solid at the bottom, as solid keeps dissolving exactly as fast as ions crystallize back out. The constant for that balance is called the solubility product, K-sub-s-p.
tossups.r: This state can only be reached in a closed system. For 10 points, name this state in which a reversible process runs forward and backward at equal rates.

clues.t: The forward and reverse reactions happen at equal rates
Concentrations of reactants and products stop changing, though they are usually not equal to each other
Shown with a double arrow (⇌) for a reversible reaction
It is dynamic: both reactions keep going even though nothing seems to change
Le Chatelier’s principle: when disturbed, it shifts to undo the stress
Its constant K is the concentrations of products over those of reactants, each raised to its coefficient
K greater than 1 means products are favored; K less than 1 means reactants are favored
Only a change in temperature changes the value of K
A catalyst helps a reaction reach it faster but does not shift it
Squeezing a gas mixture into less space shifts it toward the side with fewer moles of gas
Reaction quotient Q: if Q is less than K, the reaction moves forward; if Q is greater than K, it moves backward
Haber process: high pressure and an iron catalyst help nitrogen and hydrogen make ammonia
Brown nitrogen dioxide pairs up into colorless dinitrogen tetroxide: cold fades the brown, and heat darkens it
Can only be reached in a closed system
ICE tables (Initial, Change, and this state) help solve its problems
Law of mass action: stated by Cato Guldberg and Peter Waage in 1864
Berthollet saw sodium carbonate forming around Egyptian salt lakes, suggesting a reaction’s direction depends on the amounts present
The van ’t Hoff equation: how K changes with temperature depends on the reaction’s enthalpy change
The standard Gibbs free energy change equals negative RT times the natural log of K; at this state the Gibbs free energy change is zero
K-sub-p uses partial pressures and equals K-sub-c times RT raised to the change in moles of gas
Pure solids and liquids are left out of its constant’s expression
Water’s constant K-sub-w is 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C
K-sub-a for weak acids and K-sub-s-p for salts that barely dissolve are versions of its constant
Cobalt(II) chloride paper is pink when wet and blue when dry; heating cobalt chloride in hydrochloric acid turns it blue
Adding thiocyanate to iron(III) ions deepens the red color as it shifts toward the red complex
Detailed balance: each step of a reaction mechanism runs forward and backward at equal rates
Adding an inert gas like helium at constant volume doesn’t shift it
Contact process: sulfur dioxide and oxygen make sulfur trioxide over vanadium(V) oxide; heating shifts it back

trap.title: State, not its constant
trap.body: This answer line has close neighbors: the equilibrium constant K, a number calculated from concentrations; Le Chatelier’s principle, the rule for how this state shifts; and the reaction quotient Q, the same ratio measured at any moment. Tossups on the constant ask for “this constant” or “this quantity.” Answering “equilibrium constant” when the question wants the state earns only a prompt, and answering only “equilibrium” when a question wants the constant can lose the tossup.
trap.fix: Listen to the noun. “This state” or “this condition” means the state itself; “this constant,” “this ratio,” or “this quantity symbolized K” means the equilibrium constant; “this principle” about shifting under stress means Le Chatelier’s principle. If you are prompted after saying “equilibrium constant,” drop the word “constant.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Chemical equilibrium (accept dynamic equilibrium or equilibria; prompt on equilibrium constant or thermodynamic equilibrium; do not accept “Le Chatelier’s principle”)
